title: Technology that breaks down barriers in parasports wins Best Paper Award at CHI
article_content: Harvard’s Visual Computing Group developed BRIDGE, a simulation system that converts standard standing-basketball footage into realistic wheelchair-basketball videos. BRIDGE uses an embodiment-aware reconstruction pipeline that tracks players and the ball in 3D, then remaps head, trunk, and wheelchair base movements. The Harvard-led study won a Best Paper Award at CHI 2026. Researchers said the project was motivated by the lack of accessible sports-analysis tools for para-athletes and by the cognitive burden wheelchair-basketball players face when mentally translating conventional basketball footage into wheelchair play. In controlled studies with 20 participants, including 10 Japanese national wheelchair-basketball team players and 10 non-elite players, BRIDGE significantly improved perceived naturalness of player postures and made tactical intentions easier to understand. Participants said the system better reflected players’ functional capabilities than standard non-disabled video resources. The team said the work points toward broader uses of embodiment transformation in parasports, rehabilitation, and training for youth and older athletes.
source: EurekAlert! / Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences

additional_sources.title: BRIDGE: Borderless Reconfiguration for Inclusive and Diverse Gameplay Experience in Wheelchair Basketball
additional_sources.source: ACM Digital Library / CHI 2026 paper record
additional_sources.article_content: The ACM paper record provides the formal research framing behind the award announcement. It identifies BRIDGE as a system for transforming conventional basketball broadcast footage into wheelchair-basketball visualizations while preserving tactical meaning under different embodiment constraints. The paper description notes two controlled studies with 20 participants, split between national wheelchair-basketball players and amateur players, and reports that the system improved both tactical understanding and the realism of player movement representations. As a complementary source, the ACM listing is useful because it confirms the peer-reviewed venue, authorship, and evaluation setup, and it frames the work not just as a press announcement but as a human-computer interaction contribution focused on inclusive gameplay experience and embodiment-aware visualization design.

market_context_source.title: 2026 Global Sports Industry Outlook
market_context_source.article_content: Deloitte’s sports industry outlook provides broader market context for why a tool like BRIDGE matters beyond a single research award. The report argues that AI is reshaping how sports organizations operate, engage fans, develop athletes, and monetize digital experiences, while the sports sector increasingly converges with media, entertainment, and data-driven performance services. In that environment, inclusive analytics tools for parasports fit a wider industry shift toward more personalized, technology-enabled participation and training experiences. The report is useful market context because it shows that BRIDGE is not an isolated accessibility project: it sits within a larger movement toward AI-supported sports infrastructure, differentiated digital products, and new investment in performance technology across the sports ecosystem.
